news.source_body_en: Cervical cancer is the most common cancer among women in Thailand, with over 6,000 new cases and 2,600 deaths annually. Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is the primary cause, detected in 99.7% of cases. While conventional Pap smears have limitations, advanced HPV DNA testing offers high sensitivity (90%) for early detection. Ramkhamhaeng Hospital provides PCR-based HPV testing, combining sample collection during pelvic exams with results within seven days. Early intervention through regular screening can prevent progression, as precancerous lesions take years to develop. Women aged 30+ are advised to undergo combined Pap smear and HPV testing every three years if normal, or more frequently if inconclusive. Prevention remains key, with early detection being the most effective strategy.

MEDINDIA MEDINDIA Consult Online Doctor Courses Explore Healthy Living News Health A-Z Calculators Articles Drugs Directories Education More Search Medindia Medindia » News » Drug News » Delhi HC Lets HPV Vaccine Drive Continue Amid Safety Plea Delhi HC Lets HPV Vaccine Drive Continue Amid Safety Plea by Shravanthi Vikram on Jul 31 2026 1:29 PM Listen to this article 0:00/0:00 The Delhi High Court has allowed India’s HPV vaccination campaign to continue while keeping questions about informed consent, safety evidence and monitoring open for further examination. India’s nationwide human papillomavirus vaccination campaign will continue after the Delhi High Court declined to grant an interim stay sought through a public interest litigation. The petition challenges the rollout of the HPV vaccine for adolescent girls and raises questions about long-term safety, scientific justification, informed parental consent and the monitoring of adverse events following immunization. A Division Bench comprising Chief Justice D.K. Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia found no sufficient basis to stop the campaign at this stage. Reports on the July 29 hearing said the court observed that no “immediate harm” had been demonstrated to justify an interim suspension. However, the Bench did not dismiss the petition or deliver a final ruling on the programme’s safety or legality. It directed the Center and relevant research, regulatory and immunization bodies to file detailed replies explaining the justification for introducing the vaccine. Tamil Nadu Paves the Way for a Cancer-Free Future With Free HPV Vaccines Tamil Nadu, India, has officially taken a historic step towards the eradication of cervical cancer by initiating a free HPV vaccination drive for girls aged 1-14 years. Interim Order Is Not a Final Endorsement The decision allows vaccination to continue while the legal challenge remains pending. The court’s refusal to grant an interim stay should not be interpreted as a final judicial declaration that every concern raised in the petition is unfounded. The scientific evidence supporting the programme, its consent procedures and its adverse-event reporting system will remain under examination during subsequent hearings. At an earlier hearing on July 22, the Bench described the questions raised by the petition as important because the campaign concerns adolescent girls across the country. The court said it was not questioning the government’s intentions but stressed that reports of adverse events required careful evaluation. It consequently sought responses from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the Indian Council of Medical Research and the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization. Cervical Screening Will Only be Needed Three Times With HPV Vaccine Now with the HPV vaccine, screening will only be needed three times in women. The new programme called HPV primary testing is set to be introduced in England by December 2019. Petition Raises Consent and Monitoring Concerns The PIL was filed by gynecologist Dr Sujata Mittal and health entrepreneur Jitendra Chouksey. The petitioners allege that the vaccination programme may affect the rights of adolescent girls to bodily autonomy, personal liberty and informed consent. They have cited Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution while seeking greater transparency around the campaign. The plea claims that vaccination is being facilitated through schools and public health facilities without consistently obtaining adequate informed parental consent. It also alleges that frontline health workers have been given enrolment targets, which could create pressure to secure participation. These remain allegations made by the petitioners and have not been accepted as established findings by the court. The petition additionally refers to individual medical events reported after vaccination and asks the government to disclose detailed safety and causality-assessment data. An adverse event following immunization, or AEFI, is any medical occurrence reported after vaccination. Its timing alone does not prove that the vaccine caused the event; a formal investigation is required to determine whether a causal relationship exists. New HPV Vaccine Reduces The Risk Of HPV-Related Diseases A new improved Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine called 9vHPV has been developed greatly reduces the risk of HPV infection and HPV-related diseases. Center Defends HPV Vaccination Programme Representing the Union government, Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma reportedly told the court that HPV vaccines have been administered to more than 55 crore people worldwide and are used in nearly 160 countries.(1✔ ✔Trusted Source Delhi HC declines to stay HPV vaccination drive, seeks Centreâ€TMs reply Go to source) The Center also submitted that more than 55 lakh doses had been given in India. Around 120 recipients reportedly experienced minor events such as headache or nausea, the court was told. These figures were presented by the government during the hearing and will form part of the material examined as the case continues. The court has asked the authorities to provide separate and detailed responses rather than relying only on oral submissions. Official government data show that India launched the nationwide HPV vaccination campaign on February 28, 2026. Approximately 1.2 crore girls aged 14 were identified as eligible across all 36 states and Union Territories. Vaccination is provided free at designated government facilities, including primary and community health centers, district hospitals and government medical colleges. HPV Vaccine Dose Reduced to Two Shots for Cervical Cancer : CDC Recommends Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends two dose -HPV vaccine schedule for preventing cervical cancer and infections in preteens. HPV Vaccination Targets Cervical Cancer Human papillomavirus is a group of approximately 200 viruses transmitted mainly through intimate skin-to-skin and sexual contact. Most HPV infections disappear without treatment. However, persistent infection with certain high-risk types can cause abnormal cellular changes and eventually lead to cancer. Almost all cervical cancer cases are linked to high-risk HPV infection. HPV is also associated with cancers affecting the anus, vulva, vagina, penis and mouth or throat.(2✔ ✔Trusted Source Human papillomavirus and cancer Go to source) HPV types 16 and 18 are responsible for approximately 70% of cervical cancers. Vaccines are most effective when administered before exposure to the virus. The World Health Organization recommends HPV vaccination as a priority for girls aged nine to 14. Depending on age and immune status, the vaccine may be administered in one or two doses, while immunocompromised individuals may need additional doses. Vaccination prevents new infections but does not treat an existing HPV infection. Cervical screening remains necessary later in life because no vaccine protects against every cancer-causing HPV type. Safety Evidence and Surveillance Remain Important The WHO’s Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety has repeatedly reviewed data on HPV vaccines and considers them to have a strong safety profile.(1✔ ✔Trusted Source Delhi HC declines to stay HPV vaccination drive, seeks Centreâ€TMs reply Go to source) Common short-term reactions to vaccination may include pain or swelling at the injection site, headache, dizziness, nausea or fainting. Severe allergic reactions are possible but rare.(1✔ ✔Trusted Source Delhi HC declines to stay HPV vaccination drive, seeks Centreâ€TMs reply Go to source) Large safety reviews have not established causal links between HPV vaccination and several long-term conditions that have been attributed to the vaccine in case reports. Established global safety evidence does not remove the need for transparent monitoring. A national campaign must still provide clear information, obtain appropriate consent, investigate serious medical events and publish safety findings in a way that allows independent assessment. The Delhi High Court will continue examining whether India’s rollout meets these requirements while the vaccination programme remains in operation. analysis.time: Published on July 31, 2026; event occurred on July 29, 2026, with the vaccination campaign launched on February 28, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: India, nationwide campaign targeting adolescent girls aged 14, with approximately 1.2 crore girls identified as eligible across 36 states and Union Territories.
analysis.event: The Delhi High Court declined to grant an interim stay on India’s HPV vaccination campaign, allowing it to continue while questions about informed consent, safety evidence, and monitoring remain under examination.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Over 55 lakh doses administered in India; approximately 120 recipients reported minor events such as headache or nausea; no immediate harm demonstrated to justify suspension; campaign targets cervical cancer prevention.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Court directed the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Indian Council of Medical Research, and Central Drugs Standard Control Organization to file detailed replies; vaccination continues while legal challenge is pending; safety and consent procedures remain under examination.

analysis.brief_en: The Delhi High Court has allowed India’s HPV vaccination campaign to proceed after declining an interim stay, citing no immediate harm to justify suspension. The court, however, emphasized the need for further examination of informed consent, safety evidence, and monitoring protocols. news.content: 01 August, 2026 | Saturday BioPharma America BioPharma Europe BioPharma Middle East BioPharma Africa BioPharma APAC Events Media Pack Login BioPharma Pharma & Biopharma Manufacturing Pharma Research Pharma QC Clinical Trials Drug Discovery Drug Approval BioSimilar Pharma Packaging LAB LAB Business LAB Health & Safety LAB Products LAB Design LAB Testing LifeScience Biotech Biologics BioSimilar Clinical & Diagnostic Emerging Biotech Vaccines BioChemicals Cell & Gene Antibody Drug Conjugates Contract Services Contract Research Clinical Research Contract Manufacturing Methods Development Pre-Clinical Outsourcing Bio Digital Digital Health Digital CRO’s Health CIO Digital Innovation Artificial Intelligence Patent Medtech Med’s Industry Medical Devices Medical Diagnostic Bio Marketing Bio Jobs Bio Special WhitePaper Product in Action Premium Article BioInvest Bio Informatics Webinar MasterControl Resource Centre Special Report Sustainable Biopharma Mergers and Acquisitions Bio Insight Bio Analysis Bio Feature Bio Reports Bio-Interaction BioResources Consumer Health Healthcare FemHealth Focus Endocrinology Neurology Cancer / Immunology Cancer / Oncology COVID19 Mental Health Diabetes Nutraceutical & Supplement Medicine Countries Australia New Zealand South Korea Japan Malaysia Thailand Singapore Indonesia India China Taiwan Hong Kong Vietnam SAARC Countries SEA Countries EMEA (Middle East & Africa) North America Europe World LifeScience Biologics Seegene Advances Comprehensive HPV and STI PCR Testing with Large-Scale Clinical Evidence Seegene Advances Comprehensive HPV and STI PCR Testing with Large-Scale Clinical Evidence 29 July 2026 | Wednesday | News Analysis of 60,000 test results found STI pathogens in 82% of HPV-positive cases, supporting a syndromic testing approach to strengthen cervical cancer risk assessment and reproductive health diagnostics. STAgoraTM analysis of approximately 60,000 test results collected over 42 months showed that STI pathogens were detected in 82% of HPV-positive cases Findings support the potential value of a comprehensive testing approach that provides both HPV and STI pathogen information Seegene to validate the clinical utility of comprehensive HPV & STI testing through the Global Million Clinical Study and establish scientific evidence for new global standards of PCR testing Seegene Inc., a global molecular diagnostics company, announced a comprehensive syndromic PCR-based testing approach for reproductive tract infections (RTIs) through the simultaneous detection of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and human papillomavirus (HPV). The announcement follows Seegene's launch of the Global Million Clinical Study (GMCS) on July 8. The initiative aims to generate scientific evidence for Global New Standard of PCR testing by accumulating real-world clinical data from healthcare institutions worldwide and evaluating the clinical utility of disease-specific diagnostic testing strategies. HPV is widely recognized as the primary cause of cervical cancer, and certain high-risk genotypes, particularly HPV-16 and HPV-18, are closely associated with disease progression. Because screening and follow-up strategies may vary depending on the HPV genotype detected, identifying not only the presence of HPV but also the genotype provides important clinical information for patient management. STIs are caused by a variety of pathogens, including Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. They may present with a broad range of symptoms, including abnormal discharge, dysuria, genital pain or itching, dyspareunia, lower abdominal pain, genital ulcers, vesicles or warts, and infertility. Because different pathogens often cause similar clinical symptoms, identifying the causative pathogen with symptoms alone may be difficult. In addition, asymptomatic infections are common and may contribute to unrecognized transmission. Recent studies have suggested that STIs and vaginal dysbiosis may be associated with changes in the local inflammatory, immune, and microbial environment of the cervix, potentially influencing HPV acquisition, persistence, or clearance. This growing body of evidence underscores the importance of interpreting HPV and STI findings within the broader clinical context – including the patient's age, symptoms, sexual history and exposure risk, pregnancy plan, prior infection history and the specific organism detected. Together, these findings provide a scientific rationale for further evaluating a comprehensive HPV and STI testing approach that assesses HPV risk alongside concurrent sexually transmitted and reproductive tract infections. Using STAgoraTM, Seegene's real-time test data analytics and statistical platform, the company internally analyzed approximately 60,000 HPV & STI co-testing results generated over a 42-month period. The analysis showed that STI pathogens were detected in 82% of HPV-positive cases, while HPV was detected in 46% of STI-positive cases. In addition, co-detection of HPV and STI pathogens was observed in 71% of positive cases identified through comprehensive HPV & STI testing. These findings demonstrate the potential application of concurrent STI testing with HPV screening. The promising applications may include identifying asymptomatic STIs, assessing co-infections in HPV-positive individuals, and supporting reproductive health evaluations during pregnancy planning or infertility assessment. Through GMCS, Seegene plans to continue accumulating clinical evidence on comprehensive HPV & STI testing and to statistically evaluate its clinical utility and applicability using STAgoraTM. news.source_body_en: Seegene has announced a comprehensive syndromic PCR-based testing approach for reproductive tract infections that simultaneously detects sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and human papillomavirus (HPV). Based on analysis of 60,000 test results collected over 42 months, the company found that STI pathogens were present in 82% of HPV-positive cases, HPV in 46% of STI-positive cases, and co-detection in 71% of positive cases. These findings support the potential value of comprehensive testing for cervical cancer risk assessment and reproductive health diagnostics. The announcement follows Seegene's launch of the Global Million Clinical Study on July 8, 2026, which aims to generate scientific evidence for a new global standard of PCR testing by accumulating real-world clinical data from healthcare institutions worldwide.

min read Corporate media solutions Cervical cancer is among the leading cancers affecting women in Kenya. [Courtesy] Vaccines & Immunizations Cervical cancer remains one of the clearest examples of a disease that modern medicine knows how to prevent, yet too many women continue to die from it. Globally, about 660,000 women were diagnosed with cervical cancer in 2022, and roughly 350,000 died from the disease. The burden is heaviest in low- and middle-income countries, where access to vaccination, screening, diagnosis and treatment is often limited. Kenya is no exception. Cervical cancer is among the leading cancers affecting women in the country. Recent Ministry of Health figures, citing GLOBOCAN 2022, estimate about 5,845 new cervical cancer cases and 3,591 deaths in Kenya each year. That means thousands of families continue to lose mothers, daughters, sisters, wives, colleagues and friends to a cancer that can often be prevented. This is why the conversation around the human papillomavirus, better known as HPV, deserves attention. The concern is not merely about a vaccine. It is about preventing cancer before it starts. HPV is a very common virus, transmitted mainly through sexual contact. Most HPV infections clear naturally and never cause disease. The problem arises when infection with high-risk HPV types persists for years. Over time, this can cause abnormal changes in the cells of the cervix. If those changes are not detected and treated early, they may develop into cervical cancer. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV causes virtually all cervical cancers, with HPV types 16 and 18 responsible for a large share of cases worldwide. Cancer That is where vaccination comes in. The HPV vaccine is designed to protect against the high-risk HPV types that cause most cervical cancers. It also helps prevent some other HPV-related cancers, including cancers of the vulva, vagina, anus and oropharynx. Importantly, the vaccine works best when given before exposure to HPV, which is why health authorities recommend vaccination in early adolescence. WHO identifies girls aged 9 to 14 as the primary target group for HPV vaccination, before they become sexually active. Kenya introduced HPV vaccination into the national immunisation programme in 2019, initially targeting 10-year-old girls. In November 2025, the country moved from a two-dose to a single-dose HPV vaccination schedule, in line with WHO recommendations and global evidence supporting simplified delivery. This shift is important because it reduces the need for repeat clinic visits and can help reach more girls, especially in communities where distance, transport costs and time away from work or school are real barriers. Some parents understandably ask: why vaccinate girls so young? The answer is simple. Prevention must come before exposure. We do not wait for children to encounter measles before vaccinating them against measles. In the same way, HPV vaccination is offered early so that girls are protected long before they face the risk of infection. People & Society The vaccine should also not be misunderstood as a replacement for screening. It is one part of a wider cervical cancer prevention strategy. Women who are already sexually active, including those who were not vaccinated as children, still benefit greatly from cervical cancer screening. Screening helps detect HPV infection or precancerous lesions before they become cancer. These early changes are not cancer, and when found in time, they can be treated. . Keep Reading Health practitioners call for inclusivity in policy formulation How one father is leading Kenya's malaria fight State rolls out five-year plan to fight cervical cancer Pharmacy-based PrEP emerges as key in Kenya's HIV fight In Kenya, national screening guidelines recommend cervical cancer screening for women aged between 25 and 49. HPV testing is recommended as the primary screening method for women above 30 where available, while visual inspection with acetic acid, visual inspection with Lugol’s iodine and Pap smear testing may be used depending on resources and clinical circumstances. Health Conditions The good news is that the development of cervical cancer from the time of infection usually takes over 10 years. This is plenty of time to screen women who are sexually active and find out if they are carrying the virus or if they have developed precancerous lesions in the cervix, that can easily be treated, hence preventing cancer in those who have been exposed already. Screening can be done via a vaginal swab for HPV, obtained by a healthcare provider, or by the woman herself (self-swabbing), or via a gynaecological exam whereby a pap smear is taken to check for precancerous conditions of the cervix, that is, changes to cervical cells that make them more likely to develop into cancer, To do the examination, your doctor, or nurse looks inside your vagina using a device called a speculum. He/she will then use a small brush to collect cells from the cervix that will be examined in the laboratory. Alternative screening can be done via a visual exam of the cervix after applying a stain. Precancerous conditions are not yet cancer, but there is a higher chance these abnormal changes will become cervical cancer if they aren’t treated. If left untreated, it may take 10 years, or more for precancerous conditions of the cervix to turn into cervical cancer, but sometimes this happens in less time. Health This screening test is not painful and provides information that can be life-saving. Women between the ages of 25 to 64 are advised to have a screening test done every 3-5 years. However, HIV positive women are urged to undergo the procedure every year. Screening is very important even for women who have already received the HPV vaccine. This is because the vaccine does not protect against all types of cervical cancers and regular screening will catch precancerous cells before they become cancer. This is a call for girls, women, sisters, mothers...to take this seriously! Get vaccinated, get screened, get treated and don’t let this virus kill you. This is also a call to men, husbands, fathers...support your women and girls! - Prof Temmerman is a Consultant Obstetrician Gynaecologist and East Africa Director, Centre of Excellence in Women and Child Health at Aga Khan University U.S. Privacy Dr Victoria Mutiso killing: DCI detains two persons of interestDiscover Crime city? Recent Ministry of Health figures, citing GLOBOCAN 2022, estimate about 5,845 new cervical cancer cases and 3,591 deaths in Kenya each year. That means thousands of families continue to lose mothers, daughters, sisters, wives, colleagues and friends to a cancer that can often be prevented. This is why the conversation around the human papillomavirus, better known as HPV, deserves attention. The concern is not merely about a vaccine. It is about preventing cancer before it starts. HPV is a very common virus, transmitted mainly through sexual contact. Most HPV infections clear naturally and never cause disease. The problem arises when infection with high-risk HPV types persists for years. Over time, this can cause abnormal changes in the cells of the cervix. If those changes are not detected and treated early, they may develop into cervical cancer. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV causes virtually all cervical cancers, with HPV types 16 and 18 responsible for a large share of cases worldwide. Cancer That is where vaccination comes in. The HPV vaccine is designed to protect against the high-risk HPV types that cause most cervical cancers. It also helps prevent some other HPV-related cancers, including cancers of the vulva, vagina, anus and oropharynx. Importantly, the vaccine works best when given before exposure to HPV, which is why health authorities recommend vaccination in early adolescence. WHO identifies girls aged 9 to 14 as the primary target group for HPV vaccination, before they become sexually active. Kenya introduced HPV vaccination into the national immunisation programme in 2019, initially targeting 10-year-old girls. In November 2025, the country moved from a two-dose to a single-dose HPV vaccination schedule, in line with WHO recommendations and global evidence supporting simplified delivery. This shift is important because it reduces the need for repeat clinic visits and can help reach more girls, especially in communities where distance, transport costs and time away from work or school are real barriers. Some parents understandably ask: why vaccinate girls so young? The answer is simple. Prevention must come before exposure. We do not wait for children to encounter measles before vaccinating them against measles. In the same way, HPV vaccination is offered early so that girls are protected long before they face the risk of infection. People & Society The vaccine should also not be misunderstood as a replacement for screening. It is one part of a wider cervical cancer prevention strategy. Women who are already sexually active, including those who were not vaccinated as children, still benefit greatly from cervical cancer screening. Screening helps detect HPV infection or precancerous lesions before they become cancer. These early changes are not cancer, and when found in time, they can be treated. . Keep Reading Health practitioners call for inclusivity in policy formulation How one father is leading Kenya's malaria fight State rolls out five-year plan to fight cervical cancer Pharmacy-based PrEP emerges as key in Kenya's HIV fight In Kenya, national screening guidelines recommend cervical cancer screening for women aged between 25 and 49. HPV testing is recommended as the primary screening method for women above 30 where available, while visual inspection with acetic acid, visual inspection with Lugol’s iodine and Pap smear testing may be used depending on resources and clinical circumstances. Health Conditions The good news is that the development of cervical cancer from the time of infection usually takes over 10 years. This is plenty of time to screen women who are sexually active and find out if they are carrying the virus or if they have developed precancerous lesions in the cervix, that can easily be treated, hence preventing cancer in those who have been exposed already. Screening can be done via a vaginal swab for HPV, obtained by a healthcare provider, or by the woman herself (self-swabbing), or via a gynaecological exam whereby a pap smear is taken to check for precancerous conditions of the cervix, that is, changes to cervical cells that make them more likely to develop into cancer, To do the examination, your doctor, or nurse looks inside your vagina using a device called a speculum. He/she will then use a small brush to collect cells from the cervix that will be examined in the laboratory. Alternative screening can be done via a visual exam of the cervix after applying a stain. Precancerous conditions are not yet cancer, but there is a higher chance these abnormal changes will become cervical cancer if they aren’t treated. If left untreated, it may take 10 years, or more for precancerous conditions of the cervix to turn into cervical cancer, but sometimes this happens in less time. Health This screening test is not painful and provides information that can be life-saving. Women between the ages of 25 to 64 are advised to have a screening test done every 3-5 years. However, HIV positive women are urged to undergo the procedure every year. Screening is very important even for women who have already received the HPV vaccine. This is because the vaccine does not protect against all types of cervical cancers and regular screening will catch precancerous cells before they become cancer. This is a call for girls, women, sisters, mothers...to take this seriously! Get vaccinated, get screened, get treated and don’t let this virus kill you. This is also a call to men, husbands, fathers...support your women and girls! - Prof Temmerman is a Consultant Obstetrician Gynaecologist and East Africa Director, Centre of Excellence in Women and Child Health at Aga Khan University U.S. Privacy Dr Victoria Mutiso killing: DCI detains two persons of interestDiscover Crime city? New Cervical Cancer Pill Could Stop HPV Before Cancer follow usfollow us A promising new oral cervical cancer pill could transform the way doctors treat one of the world's most common cancers affecting women. Researchers have developed an experimental therapy called SHetA2, which targets the cancer-causing proteins of the human papillomavirus (HPV) before they trigger cervical cancer. Although the capsule cannot prevent HPV infection, scientists say it may stop persistent HPV infections from progressing into precancerous lesions or cervical cancer - offering hope to thousands of women, particularly in countries like India where the disease remains a major public health challenge. Breaking It Down How does the HPV vaccine prevent cervical cancer? What are the key age recommendations for HPV vaccination? What impact does the HPV vaccine have on cervical cancer statistics? Created with AI. Also read: World Hepatitis Day: 5 Dangerous Myths That Could Delay a Life-Saving Diagnosis Why is this breakthrough important? According to the Global Cancer Observatory, cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among women in India, with more than 79,000 new cases and over 36,000 deaths reported in 2024. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV strains is responsible for nearly 85 per cent of cervical cancer cases. While HPV vaccination can prevent infection, many women are diagnosed after the virus has already caused changes in cervical cells. Researchers believe SHetA2 could fill this treatment gap. How does the SHetA2 pill work? SHetA2 is a small-molecule oral therapy, meaning it is made from chemically manufactured compounds that are easily absorbed by the body and are generally less expensive to produce than biologic drugs. According to experts, the drug works by disrupting the interaction between the HPV-E7 protein and a protective protein inside human cells. Normally, this interaction allows the HPV virus to continue damaging healthy cervical cells. SHetA2 breaks this connection, enabling the body's natural defence mechanisms to destroy the harmful viral protein. Importantly, the therapy appears to target cancerous cells while leaving healthy cells largely unaffected, reducing the likelihood of widespread damage to normal tissue. Who could benefit? The treatment is not intended for preventing HPV infection. Instead, researchers believe it may benefit women who have already developed high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) - precancerous cervical lesions that have a high risk of progressing to cancer if left untreated. It may also eventually be used for patients with early-stage invasive cervical cancer, although larger clinical trials are needed to determine exactly which patients will benefit the most. What stage is the drug at? The therapy was developed by the Stephenson Cancer Center at the University of Oklahoma, with preclinical evaluation and validation carried out by ICMR-NICPR. After encouraging laboratory and early clinical findings, the technology has been transferred to Emcure Pharmaceuticals, which will oversee larger human clinical trials before seeking regulatory approval. Researchers estimate that these trials could take up to five years before the medicine becomes widely available. Will it be affordable? The final price has not yet been announced. However, because SHetA2 is an oral small-molecule medicine, experts expect it to be considerably more affordable than many advanced biologic or immunotherapy-based cancer treatments. Since it may eventually be taken at home, the pill could also reduce the need for prolonged hospital visits and infusion-based therapies. Does this replace HPV vaccination or screening? Absolutely not. Doctors stress that HPV vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent cervical cancer. India's national immunisation programme now includes HPV vaccination for eligible adolescent girls. New Cervical Cancer Pill Could Stop HPV Before Cancer follow usfollow us A promising new oral cervical cancer pill could transform the way doctors treat one of the world's most common cancers affecting women. Researchers have developed an experimental therapy called SHetA2, which targets the cancer-causing proteins of the human papillomavirus (HPV) before they trigger cervical cancer. Although the capsule cannot prevent HPV infection, scientists say it may stop persistent HPV infections from progressing into precancerous lesions or cervical cancer - offering hope to thousands of women, particularly in countries like India where the disease remains a major public health challenge. Breaking It Down How does the HPV vaccine prevent cervical cancer? What are the key age recommendations for HPV vaccination? What impact does the HPV vaccine have on cervical cancer statistics? Created with AI. Also read: World Hepatitis Day: 5 Dangerous Myths That Could Delay a Life-Saving Diagnosis Why is this breakthrough important? According to the Global Cancer Observatory, cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among women in India, with more than 79,000 new cases and over 36,000 deaths reported in 2024. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV strains is responsible for nearly 85 per cent of cervical cancer cases. While HPV vaccination can prevent infection, many women are diagnosed after the virus has already caused changes in cervical cells. Researchers believe SHetA2 could fill this treatment gap. How does the SHetA2 pill work? SHetA2 is a small-molecule oral therapy, meaning it is made from chemically manufactured compounds that are easily absorbed by the body and are generally less expensive to produce than biologic drugs. According to experts, the drug works by disrupting the interaction between the HPV-E7 protein and a protective protein inside human cells. Normally, this interaction allows the HPV virus to continue damaging healthy cervical cells. SHetA2 breaks this connection, enabling the body's natural defence mechanisms to destroy the harmful viral protein. Importantly, the therapy appears to target cancerous cells while leaving healthy cells largely unaffected, reducing the likelihood of widespread damage to normal tissue. Who could benefit? The treatment is not intended for preventing HPV infection. Instead, researchers believe it may benefit women who have already developed high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) - precancerous cervical lesions that have a high risk of progressing to cancer if left untreated. It may also eventually be used for patients with early-stage invasive cervical cancer, although larger clinical trials are needed to determine exactly which patients will benefit the most. What stage is the drug at? The therapy was developed by the Stephenson Cancer Center at the University of Oklahoma, with preclinical evaluation and validation carried out by ICMR-NICPR. After encouraging laboratory and early clinical findings, the technology has been transferred to Emcure Pharmaceuticals, which will oversee larger human clinical trials before seeking regulatory approval. Researchers estimate that these trials could take up to five years before the medicine becomes widely available. Will it be affordable? The final price has not yet been announced. However, because SHetA2 is an oral small-molecule medicine, experts expect it to be considerably more affordable than many advanced biologic or immunotherapy-based cancer treatments. Since it may eventually be taken at home, the pill could also reduce the need for prolonged hospital visits and infusion-based therapies. Does this replace HPV vaccination or screening? Absolutely not. Doctors stress that HPV vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent cervical cancer. India's national immunisation programme now includes HPV vaccination for eligible adolescent girls. Regular Pap smear tests, HPV DNA testing, and visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) continue to play a vital role in detecting precancerous changes early, when treatment is most successful. If approved, SHetA2 would complement - not replace - vaccination and screening programmes. New cervical cancer pill shows promise by stopping HPV from turning cancerous: How it works? India has taken a significant step towards preventing cervical cancer with SHetA2, a first-in-class anti-HPV drug candidate licensed by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) to Emcure Pharmaceuticals. Written By: Satata Karmakar | Published : July 30, 2026 9:41 AM IST Share Share Article ✕ Copied Medically Verified By: Prof. Dr. Suresh Babu New cervical cancer pill shows promise by stopping HPV from turning cancerous A new oral medication that may hold great promise in the battle against cervical cancer is currently under development. Researchers are working on a new drug known as SHetA2, which has shown positive results in preventing the occurrence of chronic infections from human papillomavirus (HPV) from transforming into cervical cancer. While the objective of this compound is not to cure HPV infection, it may help stop HPV from causing changes in cells that can lead to cancer. How HPV Increases The Risk Of Cervical Cancer Speaking to TheHealthSite.com, Prof. Dr. Suresh Babu, Director Medical & Haemato Oncology, KIMS Hospitals, Mahadevapura, Bengaluru, explained more about the HPV virus and how the cervical cancer vaccine will support patients while they deal with the odds. HPV is amongst the most prevalent sexually transmitted illnesses around the globe, and long-term infections by high-risk types of HPV account for the majority of cervical cancer cases. While many HPV infections disappear without treatment, chronic infections can result in increased production of proteins, leading to failures in normal cellular functions and a greater chance of obtaining precancerous lesions and, eventually, invasive cervical cancer. Also Read Only 34 of 200 girls took HPV vaccine at Delhi camp: Debunking myths about safety, side effects and fertility HPV vaccine can prevent up to 90% of cervical cancer cases: What every parent and woman should know Think it’s just period issues? Expert warns these 5 signs could be cervical cancer How The New SHetA2 Pill Works Against Cervical Cancer Unlike existing preventive treatments, SHetA2 functions in a different manner. Instead of acting against HPV itself, the new oral treatment is created to interfere with the action of a cancer-inducing protein released by the long-term HPV infection chain. Consequently, by preventing such actions, the scientists believe that their medication may stop the abnormal cervical cells from converting into cancerous or precancerous ones. While these findings seem promising, experts advise that this is still a work in progress and further clinical trials need to be conducted to establish the long-term safety, effectiveness, and appropriateness of this medication. The drug is currently in a Phase 1 clinical study and has shown promising results at this early stage. However, Phase 2 and Phase 3 clinical trials are yet to be completed before it can be approved for routine clinical use. Until then, it should not be considered a substitute for existing cervical cancer preventive measures. Cervical cancer is one of the very few types of cancer that can actually be prevented. Vaccination against HPV leads to a decreased likelihood of being infected with the dangerous virus strains, especially if performed before contracting the virus. Regular cervical screening, including Pap tests and testing for HPV, is equally important, as it allows for early diagnosis of the precancerous changes when treatment is most effective. You may like to read Why Cervical Cancer Remains A Major Health Concern In India Indian society badly needs better prevention methods, as cervical cancer is still a big threat. According to estimations by the Global Cancer Observatory, in 2024, 79,000 cases of cervical cancer were diagnosed, and 36,000 women died of cervical cancer. The disease ranks second among cancers detected in women in India and affects one out of ten women in the population in India. The development of an effective oral treatment may benefit women with chronic HPV infections and abnormal cells in the cervix, especially in places where specialized treatment is not available. Still, many experts claim that awareness, vaccination, routine screening, and timely follow-up are the most effective tools in fighting the disease. With further research on SHetA2, one more defense against cervical cancer may become possible. If future research proves its effectiveness, the medication may provide additional defense against this type of cancer. Researchers are working on a new drug known as SHetA2, which has shown positive results in preventing the occurrence of chronic infections from human papillomavirus (HPV) from transforming into cervical cancer. While the objective of this compound is not to cure HPV infection, it may help stop HPV from causing changes in cells that can lead to cancer. How HPV Increases The Risk Of Cervical Cancer Speaking to TheHealthSite.com, Prof. Dr. Suresh Babu, Director Medical & Haemato Oncology, KIMS Hospitals, Mahadevapura, Bengaluru, explained more about the HPV virus and how the cervical cancer vaccine will support patients while they deal with the odds. HPV is amongst the most prevalent sexually transmitted illnesses around the globe, and long-term infections by high-risk types of HPV account for the majority of cervical cancer cases. While many HPV infections disappear without treatment, chronic infections can result in increased production of proteins, leading to failures in normal cellular functions and a greater chance of obtaining precancerous lesions and, eventually, invasive cervical cancer. Expert warns these 5 signs could be cervical cancer How The New SHetA2 Pill Works Against Cervical Cancer Unlike existing preventive treatments, SHetA2 functions in a different manner. Instead of acting against HPV itself, the new oral treatment is created to interfere with the action of a cancer-inducing protein released by the long-term HPV infection chain. Consequently, by preventing such actions, the scientists believe that their medication may stop the abnormal cervical cells from converting into cancerous or precancerous ones. While these findings seem promising, experts advise that this is still a work in progress and further clinical trials need to be conducted to establish the long-term safety, effectiveness, and appropriateness of this medication. The drug is currently in a Phase 1 clinical study and has shown promising results at this early stage. However, Phase 2 and Phase 3 clinical trials are yet to be completed before it can be approved for routine clinical use. Until then, it should not be considered a substitute for existing cervical cancer preventive measures. Cervical cancer is one of the very few types of cancer that can actually be prevented. Vaccination against HPV leads to a decreased likelihood of being infected with the dangerous virus strains, especially if performed before contracting the virus. Regular cervical screening, including Pap tests and testing for HPV, is equally important, as it allows for early diagnosis of the precancerous changes when treatment is most effective. You may like to read Why Cervical Cancer Remains A Major Health Concern In India Indian society badly needs better prevention methods, as cervical cancer is still a big threat. According to estimations by the Global Cancer Observatory, in 2024, 79,000 cases of cervical cancer were diagnosed, and 36,000 women died of cervical cancer. The disease ranks second among cancers detected in women in India and affects one out of ten women in the population in India. The development of an effective oral treatment may benefit women with chronic HPV infections and abnormal cells in the cervix, especially in places where specialized treatment is not available. Still, many experts claim that awareness, vaccination, routine screening, and timely follow-up are the most effective tools in fighting the disease. With further research on SHetA2, one more defense against cervical cancer may become possible. If future research proves its effectiveness, the medication may provide additional defense against this type of cancer. Written By: Muskan Gupta | Published : July 29, 2026 7:15 PM IST Share Share Article ✕ Copied Only 34 of 200 girls took HPV vaccine at Delhi camp (Image AI Generated) In a recent free HPV vaccination drive in Delhi, a significant hurdle facing the fight against cervical cancer emerged: that of vaccine hesitancy among parents. Of those who were eligible and came to camp about 200 girls participated, but only 34 of them were vaccinated with the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine, with many of the children's parents stating that they had concerns about the trial, possible side effects or fertility issues. Despite evidence as solid as possible and the fact that HPV vaccination is safe and sound, there are still several major eradication myths and misconceptions preventing families from making informed choices about choosing to help prevent HPV-related cancers in children. Why HPV vaccination is important for children? HPV is a typical virus that can infect men and women. The most dangerous strains of HPV are known as HPV-16 and HPV-18, and they cause most of the cervical cancer cases. A persistent infection with HPV can also lead to the development of cancers of the vagina, vulva, anus, penis and throat. Also Read New cervical cancer pill shows promise by stopping HPV from turning cancerous: How it works? HPV vaccine can prevent up to 90% of cervical cancer cases: What every parent and woman should know Who needs HPV vaccine? Expert answers amid India’s immunization push HPV vaccination is endorsed by the World Health Organization (WHO) as a crucial approach in the fight against cervical cancer. The best way to do this is to administer HPV vaccines to women before they contract HPV infection, according to WHO. Keep in mind that the World Health Organization affirms that vaccines against HPV are safe. Vaccine myths continue to influence parents' decisions Many parents did not fear the shot or the needle, but appeared anxious about rumors that the HPV vaccine would cause fertility issues or parliamentary maturity and could have other negative health effects, according to physicians at the vaccination camp in Delhi. This is not a scientific issue and the concerns are not supported by the scientific research, says the experts. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) HPV vaccine safety data, over 15 years of monitoring and research have demonstrated the safety of HPV vaccines. You may like to read What research says about HPV vaccine safety? There is substantial vaccine safety data pertaining to HPV vaccines. In a report from over 160 studies, including the CDC's, HPV vaccines were seen to have a good safety profile. Side effects are typically minor and brief, such as pain, redness or swelling in the injection area, headache, dizziness or fever. The vaccine will not contain its own virus and will not lead to an infection or cancer of the cervix. Rather, it conveys the immune system on how to identify and combat HPV strains that are associated with cancer. Fighting misinformation with awareness More vernacular communication between healthcare providers and families will be integral to increasing vaccine uptake, doctors say. According to them, it is parents' job to trust information from trusted medical organisations, rather than hearsay or unverified statements on social media. Low enforcement in Delhi camp reminds us that mere access to vaccines is insufficient; creating trust and ensuring the dissemination of credible health messages are crucial as well. The low uptake highlights the need for better communication between healthcare providers and families to combat myths and build trust in vaccination efforts.
